artworks.title: Leda and the Swan (panel with the personifications of the River Eurotas and Sparta)
artworks.description: In this richly figured floor mosaic from the House of Aion at Nea Paphos, Cyprus, the Spartan queen Leda prepares to bathe in the river while Zeus, transformed into a swan, approaches her. Framing the mythic scene, the artist personified the landscape itself: at the lower edge reclines the river-god Eurotas, and beside him stands the female personification of the city, labelled in Greek as Lakedaimonia — Sparta herself, the eponymous nymph who is daughter of Eurotas and wife of Lacedaemon, and after whom the city was named. Set among five great panels of the pavement, the mosaic dates to the 4th century AD and survives as one of the very few ancient images in which Sparte appears in personified form, embodying the land of Lacedaemon as the genealogical ancestor of its royal line.

artworks.title: Eurotas and Lakedaimonia (Sparte) mosaic
artworks.description: Late Antique mosaic in the Hatay Archaeology Museum, Antakya (inv. 826): facing personifications labelled Eurotas and Lakedaimonia — the river-king and the land named for his daughter Sparte, wife of Lacedaemon and eponym of the city of Sparta. Far from Laconia, the pair still travels as an emblem of Sparta's mythic geography, giving the eponymous nymph a second ancient likeness beside her father.

artworks.title: Eurotas and Lakedaimonia mosaic (alternate view)
artworks.description: An earlier photograph of the same Antiochene pavement (Hatay Archaeology Museum, inv. 826), taken when the tesserae still sat in a different gallery light. The paired river-god and Lakedaimonia remain the clearest Late Antique image of Sparte's land-personification outside Cyprus — Eurotas and the city named for his daughter held in one emblematic couple.
